stem: It has been hypothesised that using an artificial sweetener that has been available for the past 15 years increases the incidence of type II diabetes. What is the optimal way to study its impact on diabetes risk?
options: 12-week intervention study of sweetener vs sugar
Animal study in rodents of low-dose sweetener
Single-dose study in humans with glucose tolerance testing
explanation:
Cohort study
A cohort study is the most appropriate way to study the impact of an artificial sweetener on glucose control over time. Several cohorts exist, which began collecting detailed clinical and lifestyle data many years ago, including data on eating behaviour. It is possible to match consumers of artificial sweeteners vs controls and determine the impact on cardiometabolic outcomes over time.

12-week intervention study of sweetener vs sugar
An intervention study of the use of sweetener vs sugar may be difficult to interpret, as protocolising eating sugar vs replacement sweetener is likely to change eating behaviour in a way that makes the data irrelevant to the wider population. There is also no evidence that 12 weeks would be long enough to show an impact on glucose control.

stem: A 73-year-old man is reviewed in the Parkinson's Clinic because of significant worsening of his motor function. He has had Parkinson's disease for ten years and is now taking three PO medications. A decision is made to treat him with subcutaneous apomorphine. What is the primary mode of action of apomorphine?
options: Dopamine D1 and D2 receptor agonist
Dopamine D1 and D2 receptor antagonist
explanation:
Dopamine D1 and D2 receptor agonist
Apomorphine is a D1 and D2 agonist with a much greater affinity for the D2 receptor. It is used as a subcutaneous infusion for patients with end-stage Parkinson's disease. Prominent side-effects include nausea, vomiting and hypotension, meaning that the dose is carefully titrated to manage these, and apomorphine is given in conjunction with an antiemetic.

5-HT2a receptor agonist
Apomorphine is a 5-HT2a antagonist rather than an agonist. There are a number of partial agonists which have indications for psychosis and depression.

5-HT2a receptor antagonist
5-HT2a antagonists include a range of agents used in the Psychiatry field such as trazodone. It is used as an antidepressant agent. Apomorphine is a weaker 5-HT2a antagonist, with a Ki of 120; it has most activity at D1 and D2 receptors.

stem: A 22-year-old man is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic. He has pain and stiffness in the lumbar spine that is worse for the first 1–2 hours each morning. He says the pain is present, but less severe, after cycling. On examination, there is limited forward and lateral flexion of the lumbar spine. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
Ankylosing spondylitis is associated with lumbar spine pain and stiffness, which are worse for the first 1–2 hours each morning. Both lateral and forward flexion of the lumbar spine is limited by pain and stiffness. Pain may be experienced after rest, and movement should be encouraged to delay disease progression. NSAIDs are the initial treatment of choice, with anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) agents as the first-choice biologicals for intervention.

Degenerative disc disease
Degenerative disc disease is most likely to result in nerve root pain, with abnormal sensation and muscle weakness on one side, which can be mapped to one or more nerve roots.

Paget's disease
Paget's disease affecting a single joint most commonly affects the hip, leading to pain, stiffness and limitation of movement. It is also associated with a significant rise in bony alkaline phosphatase level.

stem: A 67-year-old man is referred to the Respiratory Clinic with progressive shortness of breath over the past six months. He has failed to respond to high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and a long-acting beta-agonist. He is a retired stonemason and smokes five cigarettes per day. There are inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 131 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLTs) 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 29 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) 325 Reticulonodular shadowing, Chest X-ray eggshell lymph node calcification Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's shortness of breath?
explanation:
Silicosis
Given this patient's career as a stonemason, it is likely he has come into contact with silica dust. The progressively worsening symptoms of pulmonary fibrosis, coupled with calcified lymph nodes and nodule formation, fit with this as the underlying diagnosis. The constellation of X-ray changes, together with findings from pulmonary function testing consistent with fibrosis, are used to make the diagnosis. Autoimmune profiling may have a role in ruling out other causes of pulmonary fibrosis.

Asbestosis
We are given no history of asbestos exposure and pleural plaques rather than the calcification seen here would be expected in association with asbestos exposure.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not associated with the lung changes seen here on X-ray, and some response to inhaled therapy would be expected. Given the presence of nodules and calcification, silicosis is the most likely diagnosis.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is associated with progressively worsening shortness of breath and fibrosis confirmed on pulmonary function tests and imaging. The calcification seen here is inconsistent with IPF.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is associated with hilar lymphadenopathy and features of pulmonary fibrosis, but not usually with the calcification seen here. In addition, exposure to stone dust is suggestive of silicosis.

stem: A 45-year-old man with end-stage alcoholic cirrhosis is brought to the Emergency Department following a seizure. He says he has been drinking 1 litre of whisky per day but gave up 48 hours ago because he ran out of money. His BP is 155/72 mmHg, and his heart rate is 98 bpm and regular. He is sweating and anxious. What is the optimal way to manage this patient's alcohol withdrawal?
explanation:
Chlordiazepoxide
This patient has evidence of delirium tremens, which is typical in a habituated drinker who withdraws from alcohol for 48 hours or longer. Symptoms include anxiety, agitation, aggression and sympathetic activation, including hypertension and tachycardia. A reducing dose of benzodiazepines is the treatment of choice, with chlordiazepoxide as the usual favoured option. Thiamine supplementation is also essential, as is monitoring for hypoglycaemia.

Chlormethiazole
Although chlormethiazole is an alternative sedative to chlordiazepoxide, it is not recommended because it accumulates in patients with liver disease and may lead to significant sedation.

Chlorpromazine
Chlorpromazine is a dopamine antagonist antipsychotic that is not recommended for treatment of delirium tremens. Benzodiazepines, such as chlordiazepoxide, are the preferred intervention.

stem: A 72-year-old man becomes agitated on the Acute Medical Ward where he is being treated for pneumonia and acute kidney injury. He has pulled out his IV lines multiple times, is hitting out at nursing staff and is attempting to bite them. What is the most appropriate way to manage this patient's agitation?
explanation:
Haloperidol
Haloperidol is safe for use in renal impairment. No dosage adjustment is required, although caution is advised. It has the advantage of being given IM in patients who are unwilling to take PO medication. It is preferred to benzodiazepines, which are recognised to accumulate in renal impairment.

Chlordiazepoxide
Chlordiazepoxide, like diazepam, accumulates in renal impairment and should not be used here. Haloperidol, which can be delivered IM, is the most appropriate option. Chlordiazepoxide is most commonly used to manage alcohol withdrawal.

Diazepam
Diazepam, like other benzodiazepines, can accumulate in renal impairment and should not be used here. Haloperidol is the most appropriate option to control agitation.

stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed on the stroke ward 48 hours after admission. He has loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right-hand side of the face and the left-hand side of the body. He has nystagmus, and when the physiotherapist tries to get him to walk, he falls to the right. Which artery is most likely to have been occluded?
explanation:
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
The clinical features here are consistent with Wallenberg syndrome, which occurs due to occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Loss of sensation occurs on the ipsilateral side of the face and the contralateral side of the body. There is minimal weakness affecting the body. Other features include vertigo with nystagmus, a tendency to fall to the side of the lesion on walking, Horner syndrome, dysphagia and dysphonia.

Anterior cerebral artery
Anterior cerebral artery occlusion presents with dysarthria, aphasia and unilateral motor weakness affecting the opposite side of the lesion. Any sensory changes are very minor.

stem: A 50-year-old man is reviewed in the Oncology Clinic following a Whipple's procedure for pancreatic cancer. He wants to know how he will be monitored for recurrence of the disease. Which of the following tumour markers is most useful to monitor for recurrence?
explanation:
CA 19-9
Increases in CA 19-9 level are seen in pancreatic cancer and cancer of the gall bladder, bile duct and stomach. It is a carbohydrate antigen normally attached to O-glycan on the cell surface. It is primarily used to look for tumour recurrence in pancreatic cancer, rather than used to confirm the initial diagnosis. Levels of CA 19-9 of above 37 KU/l are considered abnormal.

Beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin
Beta-hCG is a tumour marker for choriocarcinoma and germ cell tumours. The upper end of the normal range in men is 3 IU/l. Its main function is as a hormone that stimulates the corpus luteum to produce progesterone to maintain the pregnancy.

CA 15-3
CA 15-3 is a tumour marker for breast cancer. It can be used to monitor for tumour recurrence/progression, with levels above 29 kU/l considered abnormal. It is derived from the mucin-1 gene. Levels are not increased in pancreatic cancer.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with complaints of an itchy rash affecting the flexural surface of both wrists for the past few weeks. He also says he has noticed some white plaques in his mouth. He has small papules, which are topped with white streaks on the inside of his wrists and some white plaques on examination of the oropharynx. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Lichen planus
This patient's symptoms fit with a diagnosis of lichen planus, with typical flexural papules and white plaques in the oropharynx. The exact aetiology of lichen planus is unknown, but it is thought to be a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease. It is slightly less common in men than in women, and is associated with primary biliary cirrhosis, hepatitis B and hepatitis C. Steroids, either topical or systemic, may be considered for cases where lesions are causing significant symptoms.

Candidiasis
Candidiasis is a cause of white plaques in the mouth but would not account for the skin lesions seen here. In candidiasis, the fungal infection generates an inflammatory response, which leads to areas of erythema and breaks in the mucosal surface in the mouth.

stem: A 77-year-old woman develops severe diarrhoea while recovering on the Orthopaedic Ward following an open tibial fracture. She has been treated with multiple courses of antibiotics. A diarrhoea sample is positive for Clostridium difficile toxin. What is the most appropriate intervention for this patient?
explanation:
PO vancomycin
PO vancomycin is the recommended first-line intervention for treatment of C. difficile infection. A 10-day course of 125 mg four times daily is suggested by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines. Vancomycin is thought to be more effective than metronidazole in treating C. difficile infection. This may be due to the high concentration of vancomycin achieved within the bowel lumen, as there is minimal absorption from PO administration. It may be combined with metronidazole in complex cases.

PO ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is not effective in treatment of C. difficile infection. For bacteria, for which it is an effective option, it is not recommended by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency where an alternative is available, because of musculoskeletal and neurological adverse effects.

stem: A 72-year-old man, who has type II diabetes, presents to the Emergency Department complaining that he is bumping into objects on his right-hand side. Visual field examination reveals a right inferior quadrantanopia. Where is the lesion that has caused this patient's symptoms most likely located?
explanation:
Left parietal lobe
The superior fascicle of the optic radiation lies deep within the parietal lobe. This carries visual information from the contralateral inferior quadrant of the visual field. As such, a left parietal lobe lesion leads to right inferior quadrantanopia, as seen here.

Left temporal lobe
Left temporal lobe lesions lead to right superior quadrantanopia, not the inferior quadrantanopia seen here, which is more likely to be related to a parietal lobe lesion.

Right occipital lobe
Occipital lobe lesions are more likely to lead to hemianopia than the quadrantanopia seen here. A right occipital lobe lesion would be expected to result in left homonymous hemianopia with macula sparing.

stem: A 67-year-old right-handed man is reviewed by a Speech Therapist four days after suffering an ischaemic stroke. He has anomia with impaired repetition, but his speech is otherwise fluent and he has good reading comprehension. What is the most likely location of the lesion causing this patient's speech disturbance?
options: Left frontal or frontoparietal lesion, including Broca's area
Left temporoparietal area, including Wernicke's area
Left temporoparietal area, excluding Broca's and Wernicke's areas
Right temporoparietal area, including Wernicke's area
Subcortical lesion near the left superior temporal gyrus
explanation:
Subcortical lesion near the left superior temporal gyrus
This patient's symptoms fit best with conduction aphasia where there is anomia, although speech is otherwise fluent, with good oral and written comprehension. Impaired repetition of speech is, however, noted. The area of damage is often adjacent to the left superior temporal gyrus, ie the dominant hemisphere.

Left frontal or frontoparietal lesion, including Broca's area
Broca's aphasia leads to anomia for both oral and written language and non-fluent speech. This is characterised by slow, effortful production, short phrase length and reduced use of prepositions and conjunctions. There is good comprehension, but repetition and writing are impaired.

Left temporoparietal area, including Wernicke's area
Wernicke's aphasia leads to anomia for both oral and written language. Speech appears fluent, taking a number of grammatical forms, but often conveys little meaning. Patients have poor auditory and written comprehension, impaired repetition and errors in reading.

stem: A 72-year-old man, who has type II diabetes, presents to the Emergency Department with acute-onset redness, swelling, heat and stiffness affecting his right knee. Aspiration of the knee reveals neutrophils and needle-shaped crystals which are negatively birefringent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute gout
Acute gout is associated with redness, pain and swelling affecting a single joint, most commonly the knee or great toe. The aspirate with uric acid crystals and neutrophils fits with gout as the underlying diagnosis, and patients with type II diabetes often have hyperuricaemia. Management options for acute gout include NSAIDs, corticosteroids and colchicine.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is more likely to be associated with chronic pain rather than with the acute unilateral knee pain and swelling seen here. The findings on aspiration are consistent with acute gout.

Prepatellar bursitis
Prepatellar bursitis, also known as housemaid's knee, is characterised by inflammation of the bursa at the front of the joint. The findings here are consistent with inflammation within the joint and a diagnosis of gout.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer and is positive for the BRCA1 gene mutation. Her grandmother never developed breast cancer and died aged 88. One aunt is aged 60 and remains well. Another died aged 35 of breast cancer. The patient's mother died of breast cancer aged 45. Why were some members of the family unaffected by breast cancer?
explanation:
Incomplete penetrance
Breast cancer related to the BRCA1 mutation is an example of a disease that exhibits incomplete penetrance. BRCA1 has a range of functions, including DNA repair, activation of transcription, cell cycle regulation and chromatin remodelling. Where BRCA1 is mutated, unchecked cell growth in breast and ovarian cancer can result. In some patients, however, there is incomplete penetrance, whereby some women may never develop breast cancer during their lifetime. Incomplete penetrance means that a proportion of people who carry the gene mutation may never develop the resultant disease.

DNA methylation
DNA methylation occurs in response to interaction with the external environment and can be influenced by lifestyle factors, including exercise, eating, smoking and alcohol consumption. It is not responsible for the variable penetrance seen here.

stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the Psychiatric Clinic nine months after retiring from his job as a solicitor. He is agitated, has no interest in activities and worries about his finances, although his wife says they have no issues with money. He appears very flat and his Mini-Mental State Examination is 24/30. Physical neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Depressive disorder
This patient has features of depression, with evidence of a flat affect, intrusive thoughts about money and disinterest in daily activities. This may have been triggered by his retirement. Symptoms lasting up to six months may be consistent with adjustment disorder, but in this case, with symptoms persistent nine months after retirement, a diagnosis of depression can be made. Cognitive behavioural therapy, with the addition of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor if required, is the intervention of choice. The lower-than-expected cognitive assessment score can be seen in the setting of depression, which should improve with treatment and be rechecked after an interim.

Adjustment disorder
Adjustment disorder is an emotional or behavioural reaction to a significant life event (such as retirement). Symptoms begin during the first three months after the event and are completed by the 6-month time point. In this case, prolonged symptoms are consistent with depression.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is reviewed in the Oncology Clinic. She has left hilar lung cancer identified on a chest X-ray. She smokes five cigarettes per day and takes dual inhaled therapy for her COPD. Her BP is 122/72 mmHg, and her heart rate is 75 bpm and irregular. Post- pneumonectomy forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) is predicted to be 0.75 litres. The ejection fraction is 44%, as measured on ECHO. What is the biggest contraindication to pneumonectomy?
explanation:
Post-pneumonectomy FEV1 of 0.75 litres
Although assessment of suitability for lung resection should be individualised, a predicted FEV1 of < 0.8 litres post-surgery is considered an absolute contraindication to pneumonectomy. Other factors, including AF, reduced ejection fraction and continued smoking, could complicate recovery, but they are not absolute contraindications to surgery.

AF
AF is not an absolute contraindication to pneumonectomy. It is important, however, to institute appropriate therapy for rate control before progressing to surgical intervention.

stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic. He has progressive proximal muscle weakness, which makes it difficult for him to climb the stairs and get up off the sofa. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day and is under investigation for a left hilar mass identified on a chest X-ray. On examination, proximal muscle weakness is confirmed and reflexes are absent. Following a period of muscle activation, lower limb reflexes are present. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's muscle weakness?
explanation:
Amifampridine
This patient has signs of underlying small-cell lung cancer and evidence of muscle weakness with potentiation. The pattern of symptoms is suggestive of Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Antibodies against voltage- gated calcium channels are thought to be the underlying cause. Treatment of the underlying cancer can lead to improvement in symptoms, and amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) is the treatment of choice to improve muscle strength by increasing acetylcholine concentration at the neuromuscular junction. It is a selective inhibitor of presynaptic fast voltage-gated potassium channels, prolonging cell membrane depolarisation and action potential, and augmenting calcium transport at the neuromuscular junction.

Immunoglobulin infusion
Immunoglobulin infusion is used for some patients with Lambert–Eaton syndrome who have refractory weakness. Positive effects, however, are short-lived, with the impact on symptoms peaking 2–4 weeks after treatment and waning thereafter.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is treated with the first dose of IV immunoglobulin for Guillain–Barré syndrome. She is concerned about the side-effects of therapy. From which of the following is this patient most likely to suffer?
explanation:
Headache
Headaches are the most common adverse effect of immunoglobulin infusion and are very commonly seen, even after a single immunoglobulin infusion. There are several headache types reported, including migraine, sinus headache and tension-type headache. Tremor, dizziness and somnolence are also seen in association with immunoglobulin infusion.

Dizziness
Dizziness is uncommon after a single immunoglobulin infusion. With repeated infusions in the same patient, there is an increased risk of dizziness occurring with therapy.

Hypersensitivity
Hypersensitivity reactions are uncommonly seen after a single immunoglobulin infusion. Following repeated infusions, however, the risk of hypersensitivity does increase.

stem: A 42-year-old man has deteriorated some four days after extensive burns and smoke inhalation following a house fire. He is managed on the Specialist Burns Ward, and the nursing staff have noted a significant drop in his oxygenation level. His BP is 132/82 mmHg, and his heart rate is 88 bpm and regular. There are extensive crackles on auscultation of the chest. His respiratory rate is 31 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 81% on air. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome
Late-onset acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) occurring within a week after significant smoke inhalation and extensive burns is well described. It fits with the development of hypoxia with inspiratory crackles noted here. Intubation and mechanical ventilatory support are indicated. Patients should be extubated as soon as possible because of the risk of developing secondary pneumonia.

Aspiration pneumonia
Aspiration pneumonia is a possible alternative diagnosis, but it is more likely to be associated with right-sided signs of consolidation compared to the bilateral crackles reported here.

stem: An 18-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with headache, neck stiffness and petechial rash. He had two previous episodes of meningitis at the age of 15 and 16 years. His temperature is 38.9 °C; his BP is 90/60 mmHg, and his heart rate is 100 bpm and regular. He has an extensive purpuric rash, with petechial haemorrhages. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 15.4 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 197 mg/l < 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 235 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Which component of the immune system is most likely to be deficient?
explanation:
C5
Complement factors C5 to C9 are components of the membrane attack complex, which is a crucial mechanism in combatting capsulated bacterial infection. Absence of C5 therefore can lead to frequent episodes of meningococcal infection, the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms. Where recurrent episodes of meningitis are seen, then prophylactic antibiotics may be considered.

stem: A 58-year-old man with type II diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with cellulitis of his forefoot. What is the most appropriate antibiotic intervention?
explanation:
Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav is the intervention of choice for cellulitis related to diabetes mellitus, because it provides a broad spectrum of coverage against Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms. A dose of 1.2 g IV three times daily is preferred for severe infection. Therapy duration of longer than 14 days is not recommended because of the increased risk of abnormal liver function associated with therapy.

Clindamycin
Clindamycin has a high level of bioavailability when delivered PO and good tissue penetration. It is an appropriate alternative for severe cellulitis in patients with penicillin allergy, although it is strongly associated with an increased risk of Clostridium difficile diarrhoea.

Doxycycline
PO doxycycline characteristically provides good coverage for Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis, but is inadequate for the typical mixed infections seen in diabetes patients. For these patients, a broader-spectrum agent such as co-amoxiclav is preferred.

stem: A 74-year-old man is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic following a barium swallow test, which showed a bird's beak constriction of the distal oesophagus. He has suffered from retrosternal chest pain and regurgitation of undigested food, including both solids and liquids, for the last eight months. His weight is stable, and he has mild iron deficiency anaemia. What is the most appropriate next step investigation?
explanation:
Upper GI endoscopy
The symptoms and barium swallow finding here are typical of those seen in patients with achalasia. Up to one- third of patients with achalasia may have coexisting malignancy. This prompts carrying out an upper GI endoscopy as the next most appropriate investigative step. Once cleared, then patients may proceed to oesophageal manometry and potentially pH monitoring. Systemic treatments include nitrates and calcium channel antagonists. Both dilatation and botulinum toxin have been used as local interventions.

Colonoscopy
A colonoscopy is usually indicated when iron deficiency cannot be excluded by other causes. In this case, with the barium swallow finding consistent with achalasia, an upper GI endoscopy is more useful at this stage.

stem: A 67-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with a random blood glucose of 18.2 mmol/l. He presented to his General Practitioner complaining of tiredness, lethargy and genital candidiasis. His BP is 128/82 mmHg, and his heart rate is 88 bpm and regular. His BMI is 33 kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 142 g/l 130–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 8 mg/l < 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 237 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Sodium bicarbonate 24 mmol/l 22–32 mmol/l Random glucose 14.9 mmol/l < 7.8 mmol/l What is the most appropriate way to treat this patient?
explanation:
Metformin
Metformin is still recommended as the standard first-line therapy for type II diabetes, given that it primarily reduces blood glucose level by acting on hepatic insulin resistance. The increase in glucose level and symptoms are relatively modest in this patient, meaning that insulin therapy is not required. This brings modest positive changes in weight and lipid levels, in addition to glucose control. The dose should be uptitrated slowly from 500 mg twice daily to avoid problems with bile acid diarrhoea. In patients with evidence of heart failure, a sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor, such as dapagliflozin, can be added in as early combination therapy.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea that can result in an increase in weight and risk of hypoglycaemia, in addition to improving glucose control. This means that it is no longer a mainstream option for initial treatment of type II diabetes.

Insulin
Insulin is not recommended in this patient as there are no symptoms or signs of relative insulinopenia. Adjustments to diet and addition of metformin monotherapy should drive an improvement in glucose control and symptoms.

Semaglutide
This patient is obese and may benefit from a glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) agonist. However, this would not be considered as a standard first-line therapy. In this patient, it may be considered as a second- or third-line intervention after diet, lifestyle and pharmacological interventions have failed to gain glycaemic control.

Sitagliptin
Sitagliptin has modest effects on glucose control and promotes a small amount of weight loss. It is usually considered a potential second-line option after metformin, rather than a first-line intervention, for type II diabetes.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with dull, aching pain affecting the lateral aspect of her hip and radiating down her thigh. She is training for a half-marathon and says running makes the pain worse. It is also painful when she lies on her side. On examination, there is point tenderness over the greater trochanter. What is the most likely cause of this patient's pain?
explanation:
Trochanteric bursitis
The symptoms here are typical of those seen in trochanteric bursitis, with tenderness over the lateral aspect of the hip which is worse on exercise and point tenderness over the greater trochanter. NSAIDs, rest and ice are the initial interventions of choice, with stretching exercises a possibility under the supervision of a physiotherapist. Where there is a poor response to intervention, then local injection of corticosteroids can be considered.

Avascular necrosis
Avascular necrosis is primarily characterised by a deep aching pain affecting the hip and groin, made worse by weight-bearing. The lateral pain suffered by this patient is more consistent with trochanteric bursitis.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department after becoming short of breath while in the crowd at a rock concert. Her BP is 148/82 mmHg, and her heart rate is 89 bpm and regular. She is anxious. Her chest is clear, and her respiratory rate is 35 breaths per minute. She has pins and needles in both hands and around her mouth. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Respiratory alkalosis
This patient's symptoms of pins and needles in the hands and perioral paraesthesiae fit with a low level of ionised calcium. This is characteristically seen in respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation syndrome, which fits with anxiety when the patient was in a crowded space at a rock concert.

Metabolic acidosis
There are a range of causes of metabolic acidosis, including renal impairment and tissue hypoxia leading to lactic acidosis, as well as other diagnoses such as diabetic ketoacidosis. The short history here, coupled with pins and needles in the hands and around the mouth, is most consistent with respiratory alkalosis.

Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis is associated with chronic use of diuretics and also occurs as a compensatory response to respiratory acidosis. In this situation, respiratory alkalosis is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred to the Dermatology Clinic because of complaints about frequent facial flushing. She says this can happen if she is in a stressful situation at work, or particularly when she drinks alcohol or hot drinks. On examination, she has dry skin, with some evidence of erythema and telangiectasia over the forehead and cheeks. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
Brimonidine topical
Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, which reduces peripheral arteriolar dilatation. This makes it an appropriate treatment for facial flushing which is associated with some more permanent changes such as telangiectasia and lasting erythema. It is given once a day for treatment of rosacea, the diagnosis here, as a 0.5% topical preparation.

Benzoyl peroxide topical
Benzoyl peroxide is a topical acne treatment, whereas this patient's symptoms are more consistent with rosacea, where the skin is dry and erythematous. In this patient, topical brimonidine is preferred.

stem: A 74-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic with short-term memory loss, gait disturbance and incontinence. A CT scan shows evidence of hydrocephalus. Where is the CSF absorbed?
explanation:
Arachnoid granulations
Arachnoid granulations play a major role in the transport of CSF. They act as a one-way valve that allows the flow of CSF from the CNS into the circulatory system. The CSF is also thought to reach the circulatory system via the axons of cranial nerve I via their extension through the cribriform plate.

Choroid plexi
Choroid plexi are responsible for the production, rather than absorption, of CSF. They consist of specialised epithelial tissue known as ependyma that produce CSF. Ion transporters lead to an osmotic gradient, which drives CSF from the circulatory system to the CNS.

Dural venous sinuses
Dural venous sinuses lie distal to the arachnoid granulations, which function as a one-way valve, allowing CSF to flow only into the venous system.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is reviewed in the Fracture Clinic following a left Colles fracture. A bone density scan confirms that her bone density is in the osteoporotic range. A decision is made to treat her with ibandronate. What is the mode of action of ibandronate?
explanation:
Impairment of osteoclast bone adherence
The primary mode of action of bisphosphonates is to inhibit osteoclast adherence to bone. They adhere to the hydroxyapatite binding sites on bone, especially where there is active resorption. When they are taken up by osteoclasts, they interfere with the ability of the osteoclasts to form a ruffled border, which is essential for bone resorption, thereby inhibiting osteoclast activity. Bisphosphonates are poorly absorbed, necessitating administration of large doses PO, and have a very prolonged duration of action.

Calcimimetic
Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic used to treat tertiary hyperparathyroidism that is unsuitable for surgical intervention. It does not have a role in treatment of osteoporosis.

Inhibition of osteoblast activity
Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast activity. Inhibiting osteoblast activity would accelerate the loss of bone mineral density. Teriparatide, a synthetic parathyroid hormone analogue, upregulates osteoblast activity and is used in treatment of severe osteoporosis.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe lethargy, widespread bruising and bleeding from his mouth. He says he has had deteriorating health for the past two months. His temperature is 38.2 °C; his BP is 95/60 mmHg, and his heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. There is extensive bruising and areas of petechial haemorrhage. Abdominal examination reveals splenomegaly. Investigation Result Normal value 7.8 g/l Haemoglobin (Hb) 120–160 g/l Fragmented red cells seen on film 22.9 × 10 9/l White cell count (WCC) 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Myeloblasts seen on film Platelets (PLT) 22 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 113 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Prothrombin time (PT) 27.2 seconds 12.1–15.3 seconds Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 46.1 seconds 22–36 seconds What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Acute myeloid leukaemia
Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) fits with the picture here of anaemia, low PLT count, a significant rise in WCC with myeloblasts and evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Bone marrow aspiration is used to confirm the diagnosis, and cytochemical staining can confirm the subtype. The usual induction regimen is cytarabine, daunorubicin and mitoxantrone, although acute promyelocytic leukaemia is treated with all-trans- retinoic acid or arsenic trioxide before starting induction therapy.

Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents with anaemia and thrombocytopenia. WCC may be high, low or normal. Bone marrow aspiration shows > 20% of lymphoblasts.

Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is associated with a marked increase in peripheral blood lymphocyte count and splenomegaly. It does not fit with the large increase in myeloblasts here, which indicates AML.

Chronic myeloid leukaemia
In chronic myeloid leukaemia, the peripheral blood smear usually shows an increase in immature granulocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Results of the coagulation studies here are consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation, and the blasts fit with AML.

Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma presents with chronic symptoms, including lymphadenopathy, night sweats and weight loss. The acute presentation here, with evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation, is more consistent with AML.

stem: A 35-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with extreme agitation, sweating and central chest pain after spending the day at a music festival. His BP is 162/100 mmHg, and his heart rate is 102 bpm and regular. He has bilateral dilated pupils, and an ECG shows anterior and inferior ST-segment elevation. He has been given aspirin by paramedics. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient's chest pain?
explanation:
Glyceryl trinitrate
This patient has signs and symptoms of cocaine overdose, including agitation, chest pain and dilated pupils. He likely has a significant coronary artery spasm, which may well be contributing to the ECG changes seen here. Use of IV glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) should reduce BP and control ischaemic chest pain. Guidelines should still be followed concerning the investigation of ST-segment elevation, meaning that percutaneous coronary intervention is an obvious next step once chest pain and agitation have been controlled.

Bisoprolol
Beta-blockers are not an optimal intervention for patients with likely coronary artery spasm due to cocaine abuse. In this patient, IV GTN or calcium channel blockers are the preferred option.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is reviewed in the Neurology Clinic with an episodic headache. She has left-sided throbbing frontal headaches, accompanied by blurred vision and vomiting, for three days before her menstrual period starts each month. She has failed to respond adequately to conventional analgesics and triptans used acutely. Neurological examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Which is the most appropriate intervention for this patient?
options: Rimegepant prophylaxis on the days when migraine is expected
Zolmitriptan prophylaxis on the days when migraine is expected
explanation:
Zolmitriptan prophylaxis on the days when migraine is expected
This patient has menstrual migraine with highly predictable attacks. In this situation of acute episodes not responding adequately to intervention, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends the use of zolmitriptan or frovatriptan as prophylaxis on the days when headache is expected. Given the headaches are predictable, it is illogical to give prophylaxis every day with an agent such as amitriptyline. The oral contraceptive pill is not recommended in this situation because it may increase the risk of stroke in women who have migraine with aura.

Amitriptyline prophylaxis
Amitriptyline prophylaxis is effective in reducing migraine frequency but can be sedating. It is therefore better to explore alternatives such as limited triptan prophylaxis in this situation, given the episodes are strongly linked to menses.

stem: A 72-year-old man is referred to the Urology Clinic. He has problems with poor urinary stream and is up four times per night to pass urine. He has occasionally lost control of his bladder and has been incontinent. On examination, he has a smooth, enlarged prostate. His prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is 4.5 μg/l (< 6.5 μg/l). What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Post-void residual urine volume
The symptoms here are consistent with overflow incontinence due to benign prostatic hypertrophy and urethral obstruction. As such, the most appropriate next investigation is post-void residual urine volume, which is expected to be increased. Initial interventions of choice include an alpha-blocker, such as tamsulosin, to provide short-term relief of obstructive symptoms, and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, such as finasteride, to shrink the prostate size over the medium term.

Cystoscopy
Cystoscopy is indicated for suspected carcinoma of the bladder. In this patient, benign prostatic hypertrophy leading to urethral obstruction is the most likely cause of his symptoms.

stem: An 18-year-old woman attends the Emergency Department with her parents after a collapse. She has been restricting her eating markedly and increasing her exercise. The patient says there is no problem, and that she is overweight and is dealing with it herself. Her BP is 95/60 mmHg, and her heart rate is 58 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 16 kg/m 2. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Anorexia nervosa
This patient has several features of anorexia nervosa, including a BMI below 17.5 kg/m 2, control of both eating behaviour and physical exercise and denial of an underlying illness. Individual eating disorder-focused cognitive behavioural therapy is the intervention of choice. In cases where patients need to be fed because of severe illness, then this is best accomplished via a specialist Eating Disorder Clinic.

Body dysmorphic disorder
Body dysmorphic disorder can drive weight loss. However, it is also associated with dislike of other bodily features, such as the shape of the nose, chin or ears, which is absent here.

Bulimia nervosa
Bulimia nervosa may be associated with reduced BMI. However, it is also associated with well-defined episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviour, which are absent here.

stem: A 27-year-old man who has been recently diagnosed with HIV-1 is started on raltegravir. What is the mode of action of raltegravir?
explanation:
Integrase inhibitor
Integrase inhibitors block the HIV integrase enzyme which is crucial for integration of viral genetic material into human DNA. They bind to the enzyme, stopping further entry of genetic material into the CD4 cell genome. Raltegravir is an example of an integrase inhibitor.

CCR5 inhibitor
Binding of HIV to CCR5 induces fusion of HIV with the cell membrane. By binding to CCR5, inhibitors such as maraviroc inhibit replication of HIV.

Fusion inhibitor
Fusion inhibitors mimic the structure of the HIV gp41 HR2 region. The normal function of gp41 is to allow the viral envelope to fuse with the cell membrane. By binding to the HR1 region of gp41, the inhibitor prevents the HR1 region from binding to the HR2 region and inhibits fusion with the cell membrane. Enfuvirtide is an example.

stem: A 34-year-old woman attends the Obstetric Clinic with her partner. A recent 12-screening test has indicated a high probability that her child has trisomy 21. She is particularly concerned about potential cardiac complications. What cardiac defect is most commonly found in patients with trisomy 21?
explanation:
Atrioventricular septal defect
Combined atrial and ventricular septal defects are the most common congenital heart disease manifestations of trisomy 21, seen in approximately 37% of patients. These may be incomplete where the mitral and tricuspid valves form correctly, or complete where only one valve forms. All forms of atrioventricular septal defect, complete and incomplete, require early intervention with cardiac surgery.

Atrial septal defect
Atrial septal defects, seen in approximately 15% of patients, are less commonly seen than more complex combined atrial and ventricular septal defects. Options for closure include both catheter-based methods of occlusion and open surgery, depending on the complexity of the lesion.

stem: A 24-year-old man is referred to the Dermatology Clinic with several umbilicated papules affecting the lower abdomen and the inside of both thighs. He is usually well, takes no regular medication and plays for a local rugby team. The lesions are not painful or itchy. What is the most likely cause of the lesions?
explanation:
Molluscum contagiosum virus
Although more common in children than in adults, MCV can spread in adults through sexual contact and contact sports such as rugby. It is characterised by crops of umbilicated papules, which are usually asymptomatic and clear spontaneously over a few months. No treatment is usually required, although where lesions are itchy or there are concerns about cosmetic appearance, topical podophyllotoxin or imiquimod is a potential option.

Herpes simplex virus
Herpes simplex virus is a cause of cold sores and genital herpes. The skin changes seen here are most consistent with MCV infection, which can be spread in adults by sexual contact and contact sports.

Human herpesvirus 6
Human herpesvirus 6 is a cause of exanthem subitum, a childhood disease associated with a high temperature and an erythematous rash. It can occasionally cause symptoms in immunocompromised adults.

stem: A couple aged 25 and 27 years are referred to the Genetics Clinic after having a second child with trisomy 21. They plan for a third child. What is the next step in this case?
options: Fetal DNA analysis in early pregnancy
In vitro fertilisation with embryo selection
explanation:
Karyotyping of both parents
Karyotyping of both parents is the most appropriate next step, given that a Robertsonian translocation appears to be the most likely cause of trisomy 21 in their two children. A Robertsonian translocation occurs in chromosomes that have a centromere quite close to the end of the chromosome, resulting in a particularly long arm. These translocations can involve chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21 and 22. When the long arm of chromosome 21 joins with the long arm of chromosome 14 or 15, then the heterozygous carrier is phenotypically normal, although their offspring can develop an unbalanced translocation and have a trisomy 21 phenotype. A child with trisomy 21 presenting in this way could inherit the extra genetic material from either parent, so karyotyping of both parents is recommended.

Fetal DNA analysis in early pregnancy
Fetal DNA can be detected in maternal blood in early pregnancy and used to identify genetic abnormalities. However, it is preferable to identify the potential cause of two cases of trisomy 21 before embarking on another pregnancy.

stem: A 28-year-old woman, who has severe asthma and had two previous admissions to the Intensive Care Unit, is reviewed in the Respiratory Clinic. She is currently taking high-dose inhaled corticosteroids, an inhaled long- acting beta-agonist and montelukast. She required three courses of rescue PO steroids in the last six months. Her peak flow in the clinic is 380 litres/min (510 predicted). Her eosinophil count is 0.9 × 10 9/l. (normal range 0.05–0.5). What is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
Mepolizumab
Mepolizumab is an anti-interleukin-5 monoclonal antibody that lowers the eosinophil count by between 60% and 90% of the baseline, depending on the dose used. This patient has eosinophilic asthma, with a significant number of exacerbations despite optimised asthma therapy, making her an ideal candidate for intervention with mepolizumab. In asthma, the recommended starting dose is 100 mg delivered every four weeks by subcutaneous injection. Therapy should be reviewed after one year and stopped if symptoms have not improved.

Adalimumab
Adalimumab is an anti-tumour necrosis factor monoclonal antibody. It is used in a range of inflammatory conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease.

stem: A 62-year-old man is reviewed on the Coronary Care Ward one hour post-percutaneous coronary intervention for anterior myocardial infarction (MI). He has developed a broad complex tachycardia. His BP is 130/70 mmHg, and his heart rate is 140 bpm, with broad complexes seen on the monitor. A 12-lead ECG confirms broad QRS of 170 ms, uniform complexes and atrioventricular dissociation. What is the most appropriate next management step?
explanation:
Amiodarone
Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic agent which prolongs the action potential by blockade of potassium channels. It also has class I and IV effects through blockade of sodium and calcium channels, respectively. It leads to some reduction in BP through adrenergic antagonism, but this is potentially less than with a primary beta-blocker such as bisoprolol. In a post-MI scenario, it is a drug of choice for medical cardioversion of ventricular tachycardia, the most likely diagnosis in this patient. For sustained ventricular tachycardia, a loading dose of 150 mg IV is given over ten minutes.

Bisoprolol
Although beta-blockers, such as bisoprolol, are useful in suppressing ventricular arrhythmias, evidence in the post-MI period is stronger for the use of amiodarone. In this patient, bisoprolol runs the risk of precipitating symptomatic hypotension.

stem: A 61-year-old woman is diagnosed with endometrial cancer after presenting to her General Practitioner with post-menopausal vaginal bleeding. She underwent a colectomy for a caecal carcinoma at the age of 44. Her mother died of colon cancer aged 42, and her aunt has suffered from colon and endometrial cancers. Which gene mutation is the most likely cause of this patient's two cancers?
explanation:
MLH1
This patient has hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) syndrome, also known as Lynch syndrome. Colon cancers are seen as early as in the fifth decade; uterine cancers are seen later at around the age of 60 years. Screening upper and lower GI endoscopies are recommended from the age of 20 years in individuals who carry the abnormal MLH1 gene which causes the syndrome. MLH1 encodes a DNA mismatch repair gene.

APC
APC mutations are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis and the development of colon cancer at a young age. The APC gene is a tumour suppressor gene.

BRCA1
The BRCA1 gene is a tumour suppressor gene, mutations in which can lead to an increased risk of breast and ovarian cancers in women and an increased risk of prostate cancer in men.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic because of facial flushing, chronic diarrhoea and weight loss. She has hypertension, for which she takes ramipril, and has suffered from recent palpitations but is otherwise well. Her BP is 135/82 mmHg, and her heart rate is 88 bpm and regular. She has a 2-cm liver edge, and her BMI is 20.5 kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 132 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 89 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3 −) 24 mmol/l 22–32 mmol/l Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 181 IU/l 0–35 IU/l Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 273 U/l 30–130 U/l What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Carcinoid syndrome
This patient has the characteristic features of carcinoid syndrome, including facial flushing, palpitations and diarrhoea. The hepatomegaly is suggestive of liver metastases. Measurement of 24-hour urinary 5- hydroxyindoleacetic acid is a key step in confirming the diagnosis, with ultrasound scanning of the liver to confirm the presence of metastases. Treatment is directed at controlling symptoms of diarrhoea and flushing by blocking the release of 5-hydroxytryptamine, the underlying cause, with agents such as octreotide.

Colon cancer
Colon cancer is a possible cause of diarrhoea and hepatomegaly. However, symptoms including palpitations and facial flushing are a stronger indicator of carcinoid syndrome.

Glucagonoma
Glucagonomas are associated with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and hyperglycaemia. One key feature is the characteristic skin rash of necrolytic migratory erythema, which is not noted in this patient.

Somatostatinoma
Symptoms of somatostatinoma include diarrhoea, often with the passage of fatty stools. Other symptoms, however, do not fit with this clinical picture. They include development of gallstones and hyperglycaemia. Somatostatin is also a rarer neuroendocrine tumour than carcinoid syndrome.

VIPoma
Although VIPomas can lead to diarrhoea and facial flushing, they also cause significant metabolic acidosis. The HCO 3 - level being in the normal range therefore counts against VIPoma as the most likely diagnosis.

stem: A clinical trial is launched for a novel beta-3 adrenergic agonist. Where are beta-3 receptors located?
explanation:
Adipose tissue
Beta-3 adrenergic receptors are found both in adipose tissue and in the bladder smooth muscle. Agonists of the beta-3 receptor, such as mirabegron, are available for treatment of overactive bladder. Attempts to develop these drugs for weight loss have been hampered by systemic side-effects.

Bronchial smooth muscle
Beta-2 receptors have an important role to play in the relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle. This accounts for the use of beta-2 agonists, such as salbutamol, in treatment of asthma.

Pancreatic beta cells
Alpha-2 adrenergic receptors are found on pancreatic beta cells. Alpha-2 agonists have been shown to reduce insulin secretion in response to a glucose stimulus, potentially making more glucose available at a time of sympathetic stimulation.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic because of pain affecting the plantar surface of her right foot, around 2 cm distal to the medial calcaneal tuberosity. Pain is made worse by walking, particularly barefoot, and by walking upstairs. It is possible to reproduce the pain by firm palpation over the area. What is the most likely cause of this patient's pain?
explanation:
Plantar fasciitis
The point tenderness around 2 cm distal to the medial calcaneal tuberosity is consistent with plantar fasciitis. The condition is thought to occur due to a degenerative process with microtears within the fascia. Pain over the area of degeneration is often worse during the first few steps of the day such as when getting up from bed. Areas of calcification are often seen on X-ray of the foot. Stretching exercises may be useful in some patients, as may orthotics. Local corticosteroids may bring only limited short-term relief of symptoms.

Achilles tendonitis
Achilles tendonitis is more likely to result in pain and stiffness along the whole length of the tendon, particularly in the morning and when jogging/running. The point tenderness on the plantar surface seen here is more consistent with plantar fasciitis.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department (ED) by the police, having smashed the window of an electrical store. He told the police that the government is using mind control via the television to turn him into a robot. He is known to use cannabis and has attended the ED on a previous occasion for acute psychosis. When asked to eat the sandwich placed in front of him, he shouts that he can only see dark walls and a cross on the table. What is the cause of this patient's inability to see the sandwich?
explanation:
Visual hallucination
The patient's inability to see the sandwich, and instead seeing dark walls and a cross on the table, constitutes a visual hallucination. Between 16% and 72% of patients with schizophrenia are thought to experience visual hallucinations, often constituting vivid scenes with family members or religious scenes.

Auditory hallucination
Shouting that he cannot see the sandwich is not an auditory hallucination – it is a response to a visual hallucination. Auditory hallucinations can include non-sensical voices, derogatory comments made by a third person or orders to engage in self-harm.

stem: A 23-year-old man is reviewed in the Endocrine Clinic following admission to the Emergency Department with two episodes of severe headache and palpitations associated with marked hypertension over the past four months. His grandfather died of subarachnoid haemorrhage, and his father has undergone a thyroidectomy for cancer. His BP is 155/95 mmHg, and his BMI is 23 kg/m 2. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no masses. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 139 g/l 130–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.9 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 199 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Calcium (Ca 2+) 2.6 mmol/l 2.1–2.65 mmol/l What is the most appropriate intervention to control this patient's BP?
explanation:
Phenoxybenzamine
A history of thyroid cancer in the family and death due to subarachnoid haemorrhage raises the possibility of an underlying cancer syndrome. The episodes of headache and palpitations are consistent with the episodic release of catecholamines. The picture is of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2a (MEN2a), with medullary

stem: A new portable machine is under development for renal replacement therapy. It includes a semipermeable membrane which allows movement of solvent molecules towards a higher concentration of solute. How is this process best described?
explanation:
Osmosis
Osmosis is movement of a solvent across a semipermeable membrane towards a higher concentration of solute. In biological systems, the solvent is usually water, but osmosis can occur in other liquids. Semipermeable membranes are a key component of renal replacement therapy.

Active transport
Active transport involves binding of molecules to membrane proteins, using energy to transport the molecule across the cell membrane. It occurs against a concentration gradient.

Passive diffusion
Diffusion does not require a semipermeable membrane. Osmosis usually occurs only in a liquid medium, whereas diffusion can occur across all three states: solid, liquid and gas.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to the Renal Clinic for review. He has not engaged with medical services before but requests screening for polycystic kidney disease because he has met a new partner. His father and uncle both have the disease. His BP is 152/82 mmHg. What is the most useful screening test for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?
explanation:
Abdominal ultrasound
For autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease type 1, ultrasound scanning of the renal tract has a sensitivity of 100% for detection of renal cystic disease. In cases where there is a positive family history, at least the presence of two renal cysts of above 1 cm in diameter or bilateral cysts is sufficient to make the diagnosis in patients between the ages of 20 and 30 years. CT scanning can detect smaller cysts but involves a significant radiation dose.

24-hour urinary protein
Significant proteinuria is usually not a feature of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease – haematuria is a more prominent feature. Abdominal ultrasound scanning is the most useful screening test.

CT angiography of the brain
CT angiography of the brain is not useful as a screening test for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, given that only 6% of patients have associated berry aneurysms.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is reviewed in the Respiratory Clinic for management of her chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Despite triple inhaled therapy with a long-acting beta-agonist, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist and an inhaled corticosteroid, she is still short of breath, only being able to climb the stairs once per day and walk around the house. Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) is 40% of predicted. What is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
Roflumilast
Roflumilast is a phosphodiesterase type 4 inhibitor that leads to an increase in cyclic adenosine monophosphate, causing anti-inflammatory, anti-emphysema and antibacterial actions in COPD. It is endorsed by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines for treatment of COPD in cases where there are two or more exacerbations in the previous 12 months and FEV1 is below 50% predicted while on treatment with triple inhaled therapy.

Benralizumab
Benralizumab is an anti-interleukin 5 (IL5) monoclonal antibody that depletes eosinophils. Its primary indication is to treat asthma that is resistant to other therapies and associated with a raised eosinophil count.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is referred to the Sexual Health Clinic with dysuria. She is 14 weeks pregnant. Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is positive for chlamydia. What is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
explanation:
Azithromycin
Azithromycin is the treatment of choice in pregnancy for chlamydia infection, as doxycycline is contraindicated. A regimen recommended by the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV is 1 g of azithromycin on the first day, with 500 mg on the next two days. A more prolonged course of erythromycin is an alternative, although nausea may affect compliance. Amoxicillin may be considered under the advice of an Infectious Diseases Specialist, although it can induce latency and reactivation and should therefore be avoided if possible.

Ofloxacin
Ofloxacin can be used to treat chlamydia, although it is contraindicated in children and pregnancy. In addition, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency does not recommend the use of quinolones when alternatives are available because of the neurological and musculoskeletal adverse effects of therapy with quinolones.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with recurrent exacerbations of bronchiectasis and sinusitis. He has required three admissions to hospital over the past six months for IV antibiotic therapy. He is apyrexial and has coarse crackles at both lung bases on auscultation of the chest, consistent with bronchiectasis. His immunoglobulin G2 (IgG2) level is low at 0.9 g/l (normal range 2.4–7.0 g/l). What is the most important long-term intervention?
explanation:
Vaccination
Patients with selective IgG2 and immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4) subclass deficiencies are at particular risk of infection from polysaccharide-coated bacteria such as pneumococcus and meningococcus. Vaccination is therefore crucially important to reduce the risk of infection with these organisms with associated morbidity and mortality. Treatment of any underlying respiratory disease, such as asthma, should also be maximised and prophylactic antibiotics considered for patients with recurrent hospital admission.

Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor has no role in the treatment of IgG2 deficiency. It is used as a rescue therapy in patients with bone marrow depression after chemotherapy.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the Neurology Clinic for review a few weeks after hospital admission for headache and loss of vision affecting her left eye over three days. She was treated with high-dose corticosteroids. Visual acuity is significantly decreased at 6/18 in the left eye, with a central scotoma, and the left optic disc is pale. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Acute demyelinating optic neuritis
This patient's age and symptoms, including headache and subacute visual acuity, are consistent with acute demyelinating optic neuropathy. Headache is usually periocular and worse on eye movement and may precede loss of sight. In the early stages, the optic disc may appear normal if demyelination is retrobulbar, although, over a few weeks, pallor develops. High-dose corticosteroids can hasten recovery, although they are not thought to impact visual function over the longer term.

Anterior communicating artery aneurysm
Unruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysms are associated with headaches and progressive loss of the temporal field of vision because of pressure on the optic chiasm. The picture seen here is more consistent with acute demyelination.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with ischaemic heart disease has recently been diagnosed with AF. She also has myasthenia gravis. Which of the following medications is most likely to exacerbate symptoms of muscle weakness?
explanation:
Atenolol
Beta-blockers can directly impair neuromuscular transmission and can precipitate a myasthenic crisis. They should be avoided in favour of alternative classes of antihypertensive medications such as angiotensin- converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. A range of other medications, including macrolide and quinolone antibiotics, as well as statins, can also precipitate a crisis.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone appears to be safe in patients with myasthenia gravis for control of rhythm disturbance. This is in contrast to agents such as quinidine which can lead to a myasthenic crisis.

Digoxin
Although digoxin is used for rate control in patients with AF, it does not carry the same risks as beta-blockade for exacerbating myasthenia gravis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is referred to the Cardiology Clinic with progressive tiredness. An ECHO reveals an ostium secundum atrial septal defect. Which of the following is most likely to be found on auscultation?
options: Low-pitched diastolic murmur loudest in the pulmonary area
Pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
explanation:
Fixed split second heart sound
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound with no respiratory variation is characteristic of atrial septal defects. This is because of a large increase in pulmonary vessel capacitance which does not vary significantly with the respiratory cycle, leading to prolongation of the time between A2 and P2, which hardly varies with breathing. This is more likely to be found in this patient vs mitral or pulmonary murmurs.

Low-pitched diastolic murmur loudest in the pulmonary area
A low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur implies pulmonary regurgitation related to pulmonary artery dilatation. Given the relatively minor symptoms and the small defect, significant pulmonary hypertension is unlikely.

Mid-systolic pulmonary flow murmur
A mid-systolic pulmonary flow murmur is characteristically seen with moderate to large pulmonary shunts. Given the relatively minor symptoms seen here, it is less likely to be heard vs a fixed split second heart sound.

stem: A 42-year-old man, who was diagnosed with type I diabetes 32 years ago, presents to the Emergency Department with a sudden deterioration of vision affecting his right eye. His glycaemic control is poor, with a recent glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) measured at 68 mmol/mol (< 48 mmol/mol). He smokes ten cigarettes per day. His vision has deteriorated to 6/12 in the right eye. He has a circinate of hard exudates within one disc diameter of the macula. What is the most effective next intervention?
explanation:
Focal laser therapy
This patient has evidence of maculopathy, with acute loss of vision and a circinate of hard exudates within one disc diameter of the macula. Focal laser photocoagulation is the intervention of choice, with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor antibodies as a major alternative. Intensification of insulin therapy in the initial stages may worsen the progression of retinopathy. Smoking cessation takes some time to be effective in reducing disease progression but is an important long-term intervention.

Intravitreal dexamethasone
Intravitreal corticosteroids, such as dexamethasone, can be used in treatment of maculopathy. However they are thought to be less effective than anti-vascular endothelial growth factor agents or focal laser therapy.

stem: A 17-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of suprapubic pain and dysuria. He is usually well and has no other illnesses. His temperature is 37.9 °C, and his BP is 118/82 mmHg. Urinnalysis shows > 100 leukocytes and Escherichia coli at 48 hours. He is treated with trimethoprim. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Rescue antibiotics in case of further symptoms
explanation:
Reassurance
This 17-year-old patient is outside the age period recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines on management of UTIs in children up to the age of 16. As this is an isolated UTI in a patient who is otherwise well and has normal BP, the likelihood of a urinary tract abnormality is very low. Reassurance is therefore appropriate.

CT urography
CT urography is useful to outline structural abnormalities of the urinary tract. In this case, however, with an isolated UTI, no further investigation is warranted.

Micturating cystourethrography
Micturating cystourethrography is useful in investigating vesicoureteric reflux and whether there is a significant residual volume of urine in the bladder after voiding. In this case, however, an isolated UTI in a 17-year old does not require further investigation.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with blurred vision, muscle weakness and excessive salivation. According to her friend, they went picking raspberries on a farm that is not open to the public. She has pinpoint pupils. Her BP is 100/70 mmHg, and her heart rate is 45 bpm and regular. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Organophosphate poisoning
This patient's symptoms fit with organophosphate poisoning, which presents with features of excessive cholinergic activity. The pinpoint pupils, excessive salivation, muscle weakness, hypotension and bradycardia are all supportive of the diagnosis. Atropine and pralidoxime, both of which lead to restoration of cholinesterase activity, are the interventions of choice. Staff treating the patient must wear protective clothing to prevent contamination with organophosphates from the patient.

Apoplexy
Apoplexy is used to describe haemorrhage into the pituitary gland, which may be linked with a rapidly growing adenoma. It presents with headache and rapidly progressive pituitary failure.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after collapsing while running for a bus. She was unconscious for approximately 30 seconds. She admits to two previous episodes in the last two years, for which she refused to go to the hospital. Her father died suddenly at the age of 38 years. Her BP is 142/82 mmHg, and her heart rate is 78 bpm and regular. There are no murmurs on auscultation of the chest. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 132 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count 7.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l (WCC) Platelets (PLT) 192 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 86 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria, Q waves in ECG leads V5, V6, I, aVL, II, III and aVF What is the most likely cause of this patient's collapse?
explanation:
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is associated with episodes of collapse linked with exercise and the ECG changes seen here, most likely due to an episode of ventricular arrhythmia. Where there are significant episodes of ventricular arrhythmia, then an implantable cardioverter–defibrillator is required. In earlier stages of the disease, there might not be signs of left ventricular hypertrophy. Familial HOCM is usually associated with an autosomal dominant pattern and could explain the sudden death of this patient's father. An ECHO to assess the degree of septal hypertrophy is diagnostic of the condition, where the septal wall is usually > 15 mm and the ratio of septal wall-to-posterior wall thickness is > 1.4 : 1.

Brugada syndrome
In contrast to HOCM, Brugada syndrome is a cause of dead-in-bed syndrome, with episodes of arrhythmia not associated with exercise. The usual ECG pattern is right bundle branch block.

Long QT syndrome
Arrhythmia related to long QT syndrome occurs in association with periods of exercise and episodes of high emotion. However, the ECG changes here are typical of those associated with HOCM, the most likely cause of this patient's collapses.

Right ventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
The classical ECG findings of right ventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy are inverted T waves in the right precordial leads (V1–V3). An epsilon wave is also seen after the QRS in lead V1. The condition can be associated with episodes of collapse linked with exercise.

Vasovagal syncope
Vasovagal syncope can be seen after periods of sustained exercise, but episodes are more likely to be associated with prolonged standing, excessive heat or periods of intense emotion. The ECG changes here are suggestive of HOCM, which can be heritable.

stem: A 28-year-old man who has had unprotected sexual intercourse with several partners presents to the Emergency Department with a large, painless ulcer on the glans penis. He says it began as a small red lesion and grew over the past few days. Treponemal enzyme immunoassay is positive for immunoglobulin M, and negative for immunoglobulin G. He is allergic to penicillin. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Doxycycline PO for 14 days
In patients who are allergic to penicillin but have no contraindication to tetracyclines, doxycycline is the drug of choice for treatment of syphilis. A dose of 100 mg twice daily for 14 days is recommended, but it should not be used in pregnant women who report penicillin allergy. A thorough investigation, including input from an Allergist/Immunologist, is recommended to determine whether the patient can receive penicillin safely. This is because macrolides used as an alternative in early pregnancy have a significant risk of treatment failure.

Azithromycin 2 g single dose
Macrolide antibiotics, such as azithromycin, are not recommended in the treatment of syphilis because of high rates of treatment failure. For patients who are penicillin-allergic, doxycycline is the intervention of choice.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic after a recent episode of anterior uveitis. She also presented with recurrent oral and genital ulceration, erythema nodosum and a left below-knee DVT three months ago. Which of the following human leukocyte antigen (HLA) types is most associated with this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
B51
This patient's symptoms with recurrent oral and genital ulceration, uveitis, erythema nodosum and thrombosis are consistent with a diagnosis of Behçet's disease. It is associated with HLA-B51 positivity, and cases are concentrated in the Middle East and Far East. The diagnosis is made clinically rather than by relying on HLA markers. Corticosteroids are the acute intervention of choice.

B27
HLA-B27 positivity is most associated with inflammatory bowel disease, ankylosing spondylitis and seronegative arthritis. The clinical picture here is most consistent with Behçet's disease.

DR1
HLA-DR1 is associated with seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, penicillamine-induced myasthenia and schizophrenia. It does not fit with the clinical picture here, which is suggestive of Behçet's disease.

stem: A newborn baby is identified as having neonatal hyperthyroidism. His mother developed Graves' thyroiditis in her first three months of pregnancy. Which antibodies are the most likely cause of neonatal hyperthyroidism?
explanation:
Thyrotropin receptor antibodies
Thyrotropin receptor antibodies (TRAb) bind to the thyrotropin receptor and lead to stimulation of thyroid hormone production, contributing to the symptoms of Graves' disease. TRAb can cross the placenta, which can drive a presentation with neonatal thyrotoxicosis. The titre of antibodies in the mother is linked with a risk of neonatal thyrotoxicosis occurring in the infant. Antithyroid drugs are the mainstay of therapy.

Ro antibodies
Ro antibodies are associated with neonatal heart block. They are not linked with an increased risk of neonatal thyrotoxicosis. Anti-Ro antibodies are seen in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, and when present, intensification of treatment in the mother is indicated.

Smooth muscle antibodies
Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are characteristic of autoimmune hepatitis and are not linked with thyrotoxicosis, where TRAb are the primary driver of disease.

stem: A 52-year-old man, who has hypertension and is obese, presents to the Emergency Department with severe cellulitis affecting the left leg. He says that he had an insect bite on his left ankle and the inflammation has worsened over the past three days. His temperature is 38.5 °C; his BP is 122/82 mmHg, and his heart rate is 94 bpm and regular. There is erythema to just above the knee, with swelling of the lower portion of the limb and adherent pus over the insect bite. He is allergic to penicillin Which of the following antibiotics is the intervention of choice?
explanation:
PO clindamycin
PO clindamycin has around 90% bioavailability and excellent tissue penetration. It makes it the ideal intervention for cellulitis, for which penicillin is contraindicated due to allergy. The standard dosing is 150–300 mg every six hours. Clindamycin, however, is associated with a high risk of development of Clostridium difficile, meaning that any reports of diarrhoea should drive a high suspicion of pseudomembranous colitis.

IV co-amoxiclav
IV co-amoxiclav is the intervention of choice for cellulitis in patients who have diabetes mellitus. It is used at a dose of 1.2 g three times daily. In this case, it is contraindicated because of penicillin allergy, which means that clindamycin is preferred.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is reviewed in the Emergency Department after requesting help for worsening of her mood. She has been receiving cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and sertraline for the last nine months, and having initially improved, she is now not eating and waking at 0400 h each day. She has thought once about taking an overdose. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Switch sertraline to venlafaxine
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines endorse switching therapy when symptoms worsen on an initial intervention such as with sertraline.
